procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 11, 1963, in Criminal Appeal No. 153 of 1963, acquitting the respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) acquitted the respondent in Criminal Appeal No. 153 of 1963.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment acquitting the respondent, and remanded the case back to the High Court for rehearing and dealing with in accordance with law.

directions: The appeal is remanded to the High Court for being re-heard and dealt with in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the benefit of the six-month limitation period under Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, is available only when the alleged act of the officer was done under the colour of duty, which requires a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office.

facts: A head constable was charged under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act for accepting a bribe.
The bribe was taken in exchange for a promise to weaken a prosecution case against two individuals.
The trial court convicted the officer, but the High Court acquitted him.

The High Court's acquittal was based on a technicality: the prosecution was initiated more than six months after the offense, which it held was barred by the limitation period in Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act.
law: For the six-month limitation period under Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act to apply, the alleged act must have been done "under colour of any duty" or "in excess of any such duty or authority."
The Court established a test to determine if an act is done "under the colour of duty": there must be a "reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office."
An act is not considered to be done under the colour of office merely because it is committed at a time when the person holds that office.
application: The Supreme Court applied the "reasonable connection" test to the act of accepting a bribe.
It found that there is no reasonable connection between the official duties of a police officer and the act of accepting a bribe to weaken a prosecution case.
The Court reasoned that accepting a bribe is not an act done under the colour of an officer's duty, nor is it an act done in excess of that duty.

The Court contrasted this with a hypothetical case where an officer prepares a false Panchnama (an official record). In that scenario, the act of preparing the Panchnama is a statutory duty, so creating a false one would have a direct nexus to that duty and would be considered an act done under the colour of office.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the act of accepting a bribe did not have the required reasonable connection to the officer's official duties. Therefore, the act was not done "under the colour of duty" within the meaning of Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act. As a result, the six-month limitation period did not apply, and the High Court was wrong to acquit the officer on that basis.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the benefit of the six-month limitation period under Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, is available only when the alleged act of the officer was done under the colour of duty, which requires a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office.
appellant_arguments: The benefit of the six-month limitation period under Section 161(1) is available only when the alleged act of the officer was done under the colour of the duty imposed or the authority conferred on him.
For an act to be considered done 'under the colour of his office', there must be a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution was barred by the six-month limitation period provided in Section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. (Inferred from the High Court's acquittal and the respondent defending it).
Cited the decision of the Supreme Court in Virupaxappa Veerappa Kadampur v. State of Mysore in support of the argument that the limitation period applied.

cases.case_name: The State of Andhra Pradesh v. N. Venugopal and Ors.
cases.principle: The benefit of the six months period of limitation is available only when the alleged act of the officer was one done under colour of the duty imposed or the authority conferred on him. Unless there is a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office, it cannot be said that the act was done by the accused officer under the colour of his office.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The benefit of a statutory period of limitation is available to an officer only when the alleged act was done under the colour of the duty imposed or the authority conferred on him. For an act to be considered done under the colour of an officer's office, there must be a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of that office.
obiter: In a case where it was the duty of a police Head Constable to prepare a Panchnama, the act of preparing a false Panchnama was considered done under the colour of his office because there was a nexus between the act complained of and the statutory duty the police Head Constable was to perform.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Unless there is a reasonable connection between the act complained of and the powers and duties of the office, it cannot be said that the act was done by the accused officer under the colour of his office.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if an act was done under the colour of an office, the court must first ascertain what act is complained of and then see if there is any provision of the Bombay Police Act or any other law under which it may be said to have been done or purported to have been done.

To establish that an act was done under the colour of an office, one must discover a reasonable connection between the act alleged and the duty or authority imposed on the accused by the Bombay Police Act or other statutory enactment.

An act is not considered done under colour of an office merely because the point of time at which it is done coincides with the point of time the accused is invested with the powers or duty of the office.
